transcript:
[15:00] Alex Chen: ok everyone, thanks for joining, um let's do quick intros, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE, and Priya is our SE, Priya?
[15:01] Priya Rao: hi all, thanks, i'm Priya Rao, runtime lead, i'll drive the technical bits—happy to dig into K V cache, prefix caching, hit rates etc.
[15:01] Maya Patel: Maya here, head of platform at Stratus, we own inference infra and cost targets, excited to understand impact on latency.
[15:02] Daniel Wu: Daniel, SRE, focused on tail latency and multi-tenant isolation.
[15:02] Kira Lopez: Kira, ML Eng, i'll own model integration and look at quantization effects.
[15:03] Priya Rao: cool. high level: prefix cache is basically storing repeated "prefix" token sequences and their KV state so future requests with same prefix get a cache hit and skip initial autoregressive compute; we also talk about a prompt cache where you cache the full prompt->response mapping for exact-match queries.
[15:04] Maya Patel: quick question, in our traffic we have lots of near-duplicate prompts with slight variations - how tolerant is Redwood to fuzzy matches?
[15:04] Priya Rao: short answer: prefix cache is exact key match by design; we do have strategies for normalized keys — strip session ids, normalize whitespace, tokenization-based canonicalization — but any fuzzy matching requires a higher level layer (e.g., semantic clustering) which trades correctness.
[15:05] Daniel Wu: what's the typical hit rate customers see? we've got concerns because our baseline is about 40% unique prefixes.
[15:05] Priya Rao: depends heavily on UX; for chat apps with system + few standard prompts you can see 30-60% prefix-hit for the early tokens, sometimes higher for autocomplete. For support centers with long context per user it's lower. important metric: prefix-hit-per-token vs prompt-hit-per-request.
[15:06] Kira Lopez: and does quantization change cache compatibility? we might run int8 on prod but float16 in other envs.
[15:06] Priya Rao: good call. quantized kernels generally produce same token probabilities but small numerical diffs can make KV state incompatible if layernorm/ops differ; Redwood tags cache entries with model artifact signature and quantization profile — so a cached KV built with q4_0 won't match a q8_0 runtime. we recommend pinning model+quantization for cache populations, otherwise you risk misses.
[15:07] Maya Patel: what about multi-tenant safety — can tenant A's prefixes be served to tenant B?
[15:07] Priya Rao: no, by default caches are namespaced by tenant id; in multi-tenant hosted clusters we use per-tenant namespace keys; for Dedicated pools we can expose both per-customer and global caches depending on policy but it's opt-in. important: never share raw prompt text across tenants in cache keys without hashing and access controls.
[15:08] Daniel Wu: hashing — do you do HMAC with tenant key? we need to ensure keys can't leak in logs.
[15:08] Priya Rao: we support hashed keys (SHA256) plus optional HMAC using tenant KMS-derived key when in Private or Dedicated deployments; in hosted mode we use platform-managed encryption and rotate cache identifiers periodically.
[15:09] Alex Chen: i'll add that for VPC/on-prem we integrate with customer KMS (you keep keys), and cache entries on disk can be encrypted at rest and tied to key material.
[15:09] Maya Patel: ok good. can you walk through an example cache-key generation flow?
[15:10] Priya Rao: sure — simplified: canonicalize text (trim, normalize unicode, redact PII patterns based on rules), tokenize with model tokenizer, build prefix fingerprint (e.g., tokens[0:N] hashed), attach model signature, tenant id namespace, quantization tag, and batch policy id — final key is sha256(tenant||model_sig||q_tag||prefix_hash). we also attach TTL and evict rank metadata.
[15:11] Kira Lopez: about TTL — how do you pick TTL relative to model updates? if we push a model patch every week it could invalidate many entries.
[15:11] Priya Rao: TTL is a balance: shorter TTL reduces staleness after rollouts but lowers hit rate. we recommend soft-ttl + version-tag: whenever you push a new model version you can either invalidate relevant keys immediately via a version prefix, or use soft-ttl and let them expire; for large rollouts we do canary and keep old model to serve cached states until migration completes.
[15:12] Daniel Wu: the eviction policy — LRU vs LFU? we have spikes and long-tail tenants.
[15:12] Priya Rao: we support multiple eviction policies; LFU works well for long-running stable prefixes, LRU for bursty workloads. also worth doing weighted eviction by token-length and estimated compute-cost-saved metric (evict short cheap prefixes first).
[15:13] Maya Patel: what telemetry do we get to measure hit-rate by tenant? we need dashboards.
[15:13] Priya Rao: we expose per-tenant metrics: prefix_hits, prefix_misses, avg_saved_tokens, per-route latency delta when hits occur; for Private deployments we can push these to your metrics endpoint (Prometheus) or ship to Redwood's console if you opt-in.
[15:14] Alex Chen: note on instrumentation, hit-rate calculation can be noisy during warmup; we provide sample scripts to align windows (e.g., 5m rolling).
[15:15] [15:15] Maya Patel: any security concerns with caching embeddings or state that could leak PII?
[15:15] Priya Rao: yes, by default we do redaction before caching and offer a config to exclude certain classes of prompts from cache. for highly regulated data you can disable caching entirely in Private mode. we also keep an audit log of cache reads/writes when configured for compliance.
[15:16] Daniel Wu: can we do per-tenant cache quotas to avoid noisy neighbors?
[15:16] Priya Rao: yes, quota and capacity controls per tenant; plus an admission policy that denies caching for tenants beyond quota or routes flagged as high-sensitivity.
[15:16] Kira Lopez: question about batching — if we batch requests across many contexts, does that affect ability to use prefix cache?
[15:17] Priya Rao: batching is orthogonal. we check cache per request and for hits we supply cached KVs into the batch for that sequence. the tricky bit is ensuring KV alignment in batched kernels; we use padding and mask to align different prefix lengths, and that increases memory overhead but keeps latency low. worst-case you get padding overhead — so we recommend grouping by prefix-len buckets for max efficiency.
[15:18] Daniel Wu: tail latency concerns — if cache lookup adds synchronous overhead could it hurt 99th perc?
[15:18] Priya Rao: lookup is designed to be highly async and local (in-process or local SSD) so median and tail improve with hits; worst-case if cache backend is remote, we do speculative execution: start model step while waiting for KV resolution and cancel one path on resolution to still bound latency. speculative execution avoids unbounded tail.
[15:19] Maya Patel: curious about storage: KV cache on disk vs in-memory — we have memory constraints on nodes.
[15:19] Priya Rao: tradeoffs: in-memory is fastest but expensive; local SSD-backed caches give persistence and larger capacity but slightly higher lookup latency; we use a hybrid: hot entries in RAM, warm entries on fast NVMe, cold on object store with longer TTL. eviction tiers are configurable.
[15:20] Kira Lopez: how do we reason about hit-rate expectations for our workload — we have many personalized system prompts plus user history — likely low shared prefixes across users.
[15:20] Priya Rao: in that case prefix hits are mostly per-user; you can get savings if you do session-local caching (per-connection cache) because repeated messages in a session reuse prefix tokens. global shared prefix cache helps more when system prompts and assistant persona are standard across users. we can run offline analysis on your prompt histogram to predict achievable token-savings; that's part of the pilot.
[15:22] [15:22] Alex Chen: quick interjection — we should plan pilot objectives: targeted token-cost reduction percent, latency SLO improvement, acceptable miss-behavior.
[15:22] Maya Patel: agreed, primary KPI is 20% token cost reduction and no degradation in 95p latency.
[15:23] Priya Rao: noted. Kira, your question earlier on quantization — we'll include a test matrix: float16 vs int8 variants and how cache tags behave.
[15:24] Daniel Wu: on-prem specifics — if we run Redwood Private, do we need inbound connectivity for cache coordination? we prefer air-gapped if possible.
[15:24] Priya Rao: Private can be fully air-gapped; coordination for global caches needs connectivity but local-only caching is supported for fully isolated deployments. for multi-node on-prem clusters we provide local coordination over your internal network.
[15:25] Maya Patel: what about model rollbacks and cache poisoning risks? we worry if a bad prefix gets cached and serves bad responses widely.
[15:25] Priya Rao: mitigations: we enforce validation policies on cache writes (rate limits, size limits, heuristics to detect anomalous outputs), write-through logging to audit writes, and the ability to blacklist keys. we also support signed cache entries so you can verify provenance.
[15:26] Kira Lopez: small nit: signed entries in high-throughput path may add crypto overhead.
[15:26] Priya Rao: true, we use lightweight MACs where feasible and only apply heavy crypto for sensitive routes; rest uses fast HMACs with hardware acceleration where available.
[15:27] [15:27] Maya Patel: can you show us a sample config for cache policy?
[15:27] Priya Rao: yes, i'll share a snippet — e.g., route: /chat v1; cache: prefix:true; namespace: tenant_id; normalize: [trim, lower, redact-patterns]; quant_tag: require; ttl: 3600; eviction: weighted_lfu; eligibility: max_tokens_in_prefix < 1024; exclude_patterns: [ssn, credit_card]; and a note on per-tenant quota.
[15:28] Alex Chen: Priya will send that as follow-up.
[15:29] Daniel Wu: about observability: can we tag traces with cache_hit=true and estimate compute saved?
[15:29] Priya Rao: yes, we emit trace spans and a "compute_saved_tokens" metric which equals the number of tokens skipped by using cached KV. you can aggregate cost savings.
[15:30] Maya Patel: any known issues with particular model families? we use a custom Llama variant internally.
[15:30] Priya Rao: Llama-like architectures are widely supported; caveat: any model with custom ops or modified attention can have incompatible KV serialization; we validate model artifacts during onboarding and surface warnings.
[15:31] Kira Lopez: are cache entries portable across hardware — e.g., GPU A with cuBLAS vs different BLAS?
[15:31] Priya Rao: KV state is model-architecture dependent and independent of BLAS typically, but quantization and kernel ordering can affect bits. that's why we tag by model artifact signature and quant profile; we don't assume cross-hardware portability unless run with identical artifact and runtime config.
[15:33] [15:33] Alex Chen: let's talk numbers — example benchmark for a customer with similar profile: after prefix cache and grouping by prefix length buckets we saw ~35% token saving, p95 latency improved 8-12% and throughput up to ~1.3x on same hardware because less compute per request.
[15:34] Daniel Wu: that's promising. what's the CPU/memory overhead for the cache subsystem?
[15:34] Priya Rao: overhead depends on cache size; hot in-memory cache needs approx KV-state-size per prefix (proportional to hidden_size*layers*float_size). we provide tooling that estimates capacity given your average prefix length and desired hit rate; typical numbers: 1M hot prefixes might be tens of GBs depending on model.
[15:35] Maya Patel: can you provide that tooling in the pilot?
[15:35] Priya Rao: yes, we'll include capacity estimator and sample cost model.
[15:36] Kira Lopez: for our internal rollout we also do A/B tests comparing results with and without cache — how do you ensure determinism?
[15:36] Priya Rao: cache is transparent in terms of model output for identical tokenization; we ensure deterministic KV merge and identical random seeds where applicable; but small differences can appear if you have non-deterministic ops. we recommend freeze RNG during A/B and compare token-level similarity metrics.
[15:37] Daniel Wu: are there any legal/compliance notes about caching user data? e.g., GDPR concerns for personal data in prompts.
[15:37] Priya Rao: yes, we support configurable redaction and opt-out per-route; in Private deployment you can disable cache or keep keys hashed and ephemeral. we provide data-retention controls and audit logs to help compliance.
[15:38] Maya Patel: ok good. let's talk pilot scope and timeboxes.
[15:38] Alex Chen: propose 2-week pilot: week 1 offline analysis and config tuning, week 2 live run on a subset of traffic (10% traffic ramp to 30%) measuring prefix-hit-rate, token-saved, latency deltas.
[15:39] Maya Patel: sounds reasonable. we'll target 20% token reduction as mentioned.
[15:40] Priya Rao: action items — i'll send sample config, pilot template, and the quantization compatibility matrix; Alex will run a dry benchmark on a dedicated pool and share numbers.
[15:41] Daniel Wu: we'll share prompt histograms and three canonical prefixes + list of sensitive routes to exclude.
[15:42] Kira Lopez: one more technical question — when you evict entries, do you proactively warm caches for new model versions?
[15:42] Priya Rao: we support proactive re-population during rollouts: you can run a cache-warm job using representative prefixes to prefill KV to avoid cold-starts. that's part of rollout tooling.
[15:43] Maya Patel: that helps.
[15:44] [15:44] Alex Chen: any other concerns?
[15:44] Maya Patel: just a note: we need the security doc sooner than later.
[15:44] Priya Rao: understood — we'll send SOC2/ISO notes, KMS integration guide, and cache encryption options.
[15:45] Alex Chen: ok wrapping up — recap and next steps.
[15:45] Priya Rao: recap: we discussed key-gen, tenant namespaces, quantization tagging, eviction tiers, hybrid storage, batching considerations, speculative execution to bound tail, security mitigations (hashing/HMAC, audit logging), and pilot plan.
[15:46] Maya Patel: thanks, this was super helpful. we'll upload prompt histogram and pick tentative pilot start next week.
[15:46] Daniel Wu: thanks all.
[15:46] Kira Lopez: thanks.
[15:46] Alex Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and scheduling.
[15:47] [15:47] Meeting ended.
